UNCLASSIFIED 
 
 
 
UNCLASSIFIED 
Request for Information (RFI) on Biologically-Derived Materials for Transient Propulsion 
Systems 
Agency: Office of the Director of National Intelligence 
Office: Intelligence Advanced Research Projects Activity 
RFI Number: IARPA-RFI-26-01 
 
 
Synopsis 
The Intelligence Advanced Research Projects Activity (IARPA) seeks information regarding the 
current state of the art (SOTA) in biologically-derived materials suitable for controlled transience in 
propulsion systems for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). IARPA is interested in understanding how 
controlled material degradation can be extended beyond structural components to include 
turbines, engines, motors, and associated propulsion elements. Of particular interest are 
approaches that move beyond ultraviolet (UV)-initiated or water (H2O)-initiated transience 
mechanisms and subsequently enable more diverse triggering modalities that are stable in a range 
of environmental conditions.  This RFI is issued for planning purposes only and does not constitute 
a formal solicitation for proposals or suggest the procurement of any materials, components, or 
systems. 
 
Background 
The proliferation of UAV operations across military, intelligence, and civilian domains has raised 
growing concerns about the environmental footprint of aerospace materials, particularly in 
scenarios where systems may be lost. Conventional propulsion components, and their controls, 
fabricated from persistent materials— metal alloys, engineering plastics, and advanced 
composites— can remain in ecosystems for decades or centuries. DARPA's ICARUS (Inbound, 
Controlled, Air-Releasable, Unrecoverable Systems) program pioneered a solution for airframe 
structures by demonstrating transient materials that maintain operational performance before 
undergoing controlled degradation, thereby minimizing persistent environmental residue. The 
ICARUS approach employed primarily UV-triggered photopolymers that undergo programmable 
degradation of structural components, establishing proof-of-concept. However, extending these 
achievements beyond airframes to propulsion systems and their controls reveals critical 
limitations: propulsion components operate under extreme thermal, mechanical, and chemical 
stresses; contain a mixture of material types; must maintain structural integrity throughout 
dynamic mission profiles; require materials compatible with combustion environments or 
electromagnetic fields; and face significant challenges when UV initiation serves as the primary 
degradation trigger within enclosed or shielded propulsion assemblies where UV exposure may be 
limited or absent. Moreover, there may be operational parameters where natural UV exposure is 
present.  Environmental conditions that naturally degrade materials— humidity, microbial activity, 
thermal cycling, oxidation— are often more readily available than UV exposure, suggesting 

UNCLASSIFIED 
 
 
UNCLASSIFIED 
opportunities for bio-derived materials that leverage natural decomposition pathways to control 
degradation of an airborne system. 
Biological systems offer compelling templates for addressing these challenges. Nature has evolved 
diverse materials that combine high-performance mechanical properties with controlled 
degradation pathways responsive to environmental triggers including enzymatic activity, pH, 
humidity, thermal cycling, and oxidative conditions. Examples span structural proteins (silk, 
keratin, collagen), polysaccharides (chitin, cellulose), fungal materials, bio-acrylics, and 
biocomposites that demonstrate remarkable strength-to-weight ratios while remaining inherently 
biodegradable under appropriate conditions. 
Biologically derived materials including wood, paper, gums, cottons, and waxes still play a role in 
defense related materials, but recent advances in materials science, synthetic biology, and 
biomanufacturing have expanded the palette of engineered biological materials suitable for 
demanding applications. These include genetically modified structural proteins with tailored 
mechanical properties, bio-derived ceramics and composites for high-temperature applications, 
enzymatically-sensitive polymers with programmable degradation kinetics, and mycelium-based 
materials offering tunable porosity and mechanical performance. Yet significant gaps remain in 
translating these materials from laboratory demonstrations to operational propulsion systems that 
must reliably perform under extreme conditions before undergoing controlled transience. 
 
Scope 
This RFI specifically targets the unique challenges of propulsion systems and their controls, where 
materials must simultaneously satisfy competing requirements of high-performance operation and 
controlled degradation with limited degradation of UAV capability. IARPA seeks to understand 
potential pathways toward propulsion components fabricated from, coated with, or incorporating 
biologically-derived materials that enable: 
1. Operational performance matching or approaching conventional propulsion materials 
during mission lifetime 
2. Controlled transience initiated by environmental triggers beyond UV exposure 
3. Predictable degradation kinetics allowing mission planning around component lifetime 
4. Minimal residue following transience, leaving limited environmental signature 
5. Scalable manufacturing compatible with rapid prototyping and production requirements 
Propulsion Components of Interest 
• Turbine/Engine Elements 
• Electric Motor Components 
• Auxiliary Systems 
 

UNCLASSIFIED 
 
 
UNCLASSIFIED 
Questions for Respondents 
IARPA seeks improved understanding across the following areas. Responses addressing one, 
some, or all questions are encouraged: 
Current SOTA Assessment 
1. What biologically-derived materials have demonstrated mechanical, thermal, and 
chemical properties approaching those required for propulsion system components (e.g., 
turbine blades, combustion chambers, motor housings)? 
2. What are the current performance limitations of bio-derived materials in high-temperature 
(>500°C), high-stress (>100 MPa), or chemically-aggressive environments relevant to 
propulsion systems? 
3. What manufacturing approaches can produce bio-derived propulsion components with the 
dimensional tolerances, surface finishes, and quality control required for reliable 
operation? 
4. What examples exist of bio-derived materials demonstrating controlled transience while 
maintaining operational performance? What degradation timescales have been achieved 
(hours, days, weeks)? 
Material Systems and Architectures 
5. What bio-derived material classes (proteins, polysaccharides, fungal materials, 
biocomposites, bio-acrylics, bio-ceramics) show greatest promise for propulsion 
applications? What are their operational temperature, strength, and durability limits? 
6. Can hybrid architectures (bio-derived matrices with conventional reinforcements, or vice 
versa) provide transitional pathways toward fully-transient propulsion systems? 
7. What surface treatments, coatings, or protective layers can enable bio-derived materials to 
withstand propulsion environments while maintaining transience capability? 
8. How can hierarchical material structures inspired by biology (e.g., nacre, bone, wood) be 
engineered to provide both high performance and controlled degradation? 
Transience Mechanisms and Triggers 
9. What non-UV environmental triggers can initiate controlled degradation in bio-derived 
materials suitable for propulsion applications? How can trigger sensitivity be engineered? 
10. How can degradation kinetics be tailored to match mission requirements (e.g., maintain 
integrity through mission duration, then degrade within hours of exposure to trigger)? 
11. What approaches can provide fail-safe mechanisms ensuring transience even if primary 
triggers are not encountered? How can premature degradation be prevented? 
12. Can enzymatic or microbial degradation be engineered to occur predictably across diverse 
environmental conditions? What biological agents enable reliable transience? 

UNCLASSIFIED 
 
 
UNCLASSIFIED 
Integration and System Considerations 
13. What propulsion system components represent the most tractable initial targets for bio-
derived transient materials? Which pose the greatest technical challenges? 
14. How do bio-derived propulsion materials affect overall system design (thermal 
management, lubricants, fuel compatibility, electromagnetic properties)? 
15. What testing protocols and performance metrics are needed to validate bio-derived 
propulsion components for UAV applications? How can reliability be assessed? 
16. What manufacturing scale-up challenges exist for bio-derived propulsion materials? What 
production timelines and costs are realistic? 
Research Gaps and Opportunities 
17. What fundamental research advances are needed to enable bio-derived transient 
propulsion systems? What are the highest-risk, highest-payoff research directions? 
18. Where can synthetic biology, genetic engineering, or directed evolution accelerate 
development of materials tailored for transient propulsion applications? 
19. What adjacent fields (biomineralization, structural biology, biomaterials, 
biomanufacturing) offer underutilized approaches applicable to this challenge? 
20. What performance trade-offs are inherent in bio-derived transient materials, and how might 
mission concepts adapt to exploit their unique properties? 
 
Preparation Instructions to Respondents 
IARPA requests that respondents submit focused responses addressing one or more of the 
questions above. Submissions should include a brief technical description of relevant approaches, 
materials, or concepts; outline critical technical obstacles and potential pathways to address 
them; and comment on expected performance, limitations, and development timelines. Where 
appropriate, respondents may provide a non-proprietary rough order of magnitude (ROM) estimate 
of funding and resources required for research programs spanning one to four years. This 
announcement contains all information required to submit a response. No additional forms, kits, 
or other materials are needed. 
IARPA welcomes responses from all capable and qualified sources including academia, industry, 
government laboratories, and federally funded research entities from within and outside the U.S. In 
response to submissions, IARPA may organize an invitation-only workshop for reviewing and 
discussing relevant research. Participants may be asked to make presentations based on their RFI 
submissions or associated research. Written submissions and workshop discussions may inform 
formulation of future U.S. Government research initiatives.

Audio Visual (AV) / Video Teleconferencing (VTC) Lifecycle Information Technology (IT) Support (AV LIT)

Hill Air Force Base 

Request for Information (RFI)

Overview 

The Air Force Nuclear Weapon Center (AFNWC) Intercontinental Ballistic Missile (ICBM) Systems Directorate (SD) team is conducting market research to define the scope and requirements of the Audio Visual (AV)/ Video Teleconferencing (VTC) Lifecycle Information Technology (IT) Support (AV LIT). For this RFI, Government is seeking input from industry on the capability to operate within a Special Access Program (SAP) environment. 

Scope

The primary objective of this contract is to provide lifecycle sustainment for current and future Traditional and Air Force Microsoft Teams (MS Teams) based Video Teleconferencing (VTC), Audio Visual (AV), and Information Technology (IT) hardware systems across ICBM Directorate Operating Locations in the Continental United States (CONUS). 

The Contractor shall provide comprehensive Consulting and Design Services for new and existing VTC and AV solutions, as well as for IT hardware installation. The Contractor shall also provide end-to-end Maintenance Services which include, but are not limited to, tier 3 support, decommissioning, and lifecycle replacement. 

To facilitate the procurement of necessary equipment and services, the Contractor shall follow the established Pricing Catalogue of pre-approved hardware, standard conference room hardware configurations, and associated services. Services and hardware may be requested in addition to the standardized configurations. This catalogue will be used for all purchasing and installation activities performed under this contract. Individual Task Orders may deviate from the Price Catalogue as negotiated between the requiring activity and the contractor. 

This contract requires the contractor to obtain and maintain necessary security clearances and to coordinate with ICBM personnel on all matters involving security impact and cybersecurity compliance, including the implementation and management of controls under the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guides (STIG) and Risk Management Framework (RMF). The contractor shall provide the organizational resources, both technical and functional, required for managing contract performance.

A NOTE FROM THE CTO 
To deliver on its current and future mission, NGA needs to deliver useful software faster 
and more consistently. To do this, the NGA Technology Strategy describes changes in 
approach, tools, and behavior that will result in faster iterations, more flexible products, 
and better-satisfied users and customers. The NGA Software Way is an implementation 
guide to supplement NGA’s Technology Strategy and provide additional specific 
guidance for teams building and operating software.
Our intent is to get to a place where NGA software products are designed and built 
with users, can be automatically updated in production daily, and use product-specific 
metrics to make decisions. We believe in small, empowered, cross-functional teams that 
deeply understand their users and constantly work directly with those users to deliver on 
their mission.
Implementing The NGA Software Way won’t happen all at once; we must start with 
iteratively tracking and improving these metrics and meeting each element below. As 
we do this together, and with an understanding of this intent, we will successfully deliver 
software products with the speed, accuracy, and precision NGA’s mission demands.   
SOFTWARE METRICS
The three initial metrics all programs must track for each software product delivered to users are availability, lead time for changes, 
and deployment frequency. It is important to note that NGA is not unique in using these metrics. These are three of the primary 
metrics DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) has studied over the past six years. These metrics use data from over 31,000 
professionals worldwide as well as rigorous statistical methods to study the most effective ways to develop and deploy technology. 
More information about the DORA metrics and study can be found in this DORA report: https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/
state-of-devops-2019.pdf.
These metrics provide visibility into how NGA balances speed (deployment frequency and lead time for changes) and stability 
(availability) during product development and operations. These two efforts, speed and stability, were once believed to be negatively 
correlated — increasing one would decrease the other. DORA research has conclusively shown that speed and stability are 
outcomes that enable each other and high-performing teams do better in both of these areas. This is what NGA is aiming for and 
moving toward. 
For software teams using NGA’s enterprise-managed version control and Continuous Integration/Continuous Delivery (CI/CD) 
pipeline, deployment frequency and lead time for changes will be automatically tracked within those services’ dashboards. To 
enable that automation, the recommended tagging method can be found in the appendix. For teams not using NGA’s enterprise-
managed version control and CI/CD pipeline, lead time for changes and deployment frequency must be independently calculated and 
transparently shared. All teams are expected to regularly share their metrics with teammates, stakeholders, users, and leadership. 
Eventually, teams will programmatically share these metrics to a central, NGA-managed location. 
AVAILABILITY
Availability is about ensuring a product or service is accessible to users when they need it. At a 
macro level, availability represents technology teams and organizations meeting user expectations 
about the software they are deploying and operating. Any time a user is not able to access a 
software product, that product is unavailable. Availability may be impacted by actions a product 
team itself takes or through issues with upstream or downstream dependencies. There is no 
distinction in availability to users based on what caused the issue; whether planned or unplanned 
and no matter where the issue originated, the impact of a product being unavailable when users 
need it is the same.
Alex Loehr
NGA Chief Technology Officer

Approved for Public Release, 22-195
Higher availability is better, as it means the product is accessible when users need and expect it. 
Tracking availability automatically enables teams to know when something goes wrong, giving the 
opportunity to investigate issues more rapidly and proactively. Although teams may have different 
availability requirements depending on mission and user needs, teams are generally expected to 
maintain at least 99.9% availability in production, which translates to about one business day of 
downtime per year.
LEAD TIME FOR CHANGES
Lead time for changes tracks how long it takes to deliver a feature for mission use once it has 
been developed. Lead time for changes is calculated as the median time between when code is 
committed to when it is deployed to a production environment, where it can be used during an 
actual mission (not in a test environment). That figure is measured across all commits within a 
given time period. Measuring this enables teams to understand where bottlenecks are in getting 
features to production and prioritize where to optimize. 
Shorter lead times are better because they enable faster feedback on what is built and allow 
teams to course correct more rapidly. Additionally, faster lead times allow faster fixes with higher 
confidence when there are issues, which directly impacts availability as well. DORA research 
shows high-performing teams have lead times for changes of less than one week. 
DEPLOYMENT FREQUENCY 
Deployment frequency is how often a product is deployed to production. A product team will 
do many additional deployments to testing, development, staging, and other non-production 
environments. The deployment frequency metric is specifically related to deployments to 
production, however, where users actually use the product to complete the mission or function. 
To the maximum extent possible, deployments are expected to be automated (see Automated 
Deployments on page 9), so increasing deployment frequency does not linearly increase workload 
on the team. 
Deployment frequency is a proxy for batch size. Reducing batch size has consistently been shown 
to accelerate feedback, improve efficiency, reduce risk and overhead, increase team motivation 
and urgency, and reduce costs (for more details, see Accelerate, page 16, by Nicole Forsgren, Jez 
Humble, and Gene Kim). DORA research shows high-performing teams deploy at least once per 
week.

potential to provide solutions for future SOF capabilities. This RFI is for REPTILE 26. 
This event will occur over the period of one week.    
Dates/Theme/Location:   
June 2026: Counter-Unmanned-Systems (C-UxS) – Gulfport, MS. 
B.  OBJECTIVE:  
1. The REPTILE event provides an opportunity for technology developers to operate 
and have their technology assessed by operational personnel through environmental 
scenarios to determine how their technology development efforts and ideas may

support or enhance SOF capability needs. The environment facilitates a 
collaborative relationship between Government, academia, and industry to promote 
the identification and assessment of emerging technologies. 
2. The deadline for nomination package(s) is April 21, 2026, at 12:00 Noon EDT. After 
reviewing the nomination submissions, the Government may invite select candidates 
to demonstrate their technologies at the USSOCOM sponsored REPTILE 2026 
event. Experiments will be conducted during June 2026, Gulf Coast area, and will 
explore emerging technology solutions and revolutionary improvements in relevant 
technologies. Preference will be given to materiel solutions between a Technology 
Readiness Level (TRL) of 6 and above. There is no intention on the part of 
USSOCOM to purchase or procure equipment based solely on participation in 
REPTILE 2026. 
3. Experimentation Focus: The primary intent of this event is to highlight technologies 
that support C-UxS and friendly advanced Unmanned Systems (UxS) operations. 
Experiments will be conducted in unimproved expeditionary-like conditions with a 
dismounted special operations team. Relevant networks and an Android Tactical 
Assault Kit (ATAK) capability will be available at the event for integration and/or 
operations with participating experiments. Depending on the technology selection 
some integration and/or collaboration with existing SOF technology may be an 
opportunity. 
4. Experimentation Problem Statement: Special Operators have a need to defeat a 
swarm of up to 100x, Group 1-2, autonomous drones while operating in a denied 
areas from a static position within wooded terrain in day and night conditions. 
5. Design Reference Mission: A special operations team infiltrated behind enemy 
lines to conduct a 5-day special reconnaissance mission. The team established a 
Mission Support Site and Observation Point in wooded terrain observing and 
reporting on an enemy facility. The team emplaced detection technologies and set 
up defensive measures to counter drone swam threats. After 48 hours, the team 
identified indications, warnings and their position was compromised and the enemy 
was sending a drone swarm to find, fix, and finish the team. The team’s detection 
equipment identified the threat and relayed it to the team and its defensive effectors. 
The effectors engaged with and destroyed the threat, allowing the team to 
successfully exfil without any casualties.

PERFORMANCE WORK STATEMENT FOR 
DEPARTMENT OF VETERANS AFFAIRS CAPITAL INVESTMENT OPTIONS 

FY2028 / FY2029 CAPITAL BUDGET DOCUMENTS  

GENERAL INFORMATION

Title of Project: Capital Investment Options IDIQ - FY2028 / FY2029 Capital Budget Documents Task Order 

Scope of Work: The contractor shall provide all resources necessary to accomplish the types of deliverables described in this Performance Work Statement (PWS) to assist the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) in the preparation of Capital Budget Documents to inform the FY2028 President’s Budget Request and FY2029 Budget Request, if needed. Major Construction projects and Major and Mid-Level Leases anticipated for the Strategic Capital Investment Planning (SCIP) 2028 and 2029 cycles will have been identified and will be scored using the SCIP Decision Criteria Model, resulting in a prioritized list of projects developed through the VA governance process for inclusion in VA’s FY2028 Budget Submission. As part of VA’s submission to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), an OMB300 Application and associated documents will be prepared for all Major Construction projects and Prospectuses and associated documents for Major and Mid-Level Leases.

This contract ensures VA’s ability to replace healthcare facilities that are significantly deficient in seismic compliance, infrastructure, or space through the authorization and approval by Congress of approved Major Construction projects and Major Leases. Without timely delivery of OMB300 Applications and supporting documentation, VHA’s strategic capital priority projects would fail to receive funding, approvals, or required authorizations. The services under this contract directly support the delivery of modern, safe, and accessible infrastructure that meets the evolving needs of Veterans—particularly underserved, rural, and women Veterans—ensuring that VA’s capital investments translate into improved access, reduced service gaps, and enhanced quality of care.

This contract builds upon more than a decade of programmatic support under similar scopes, benefiting from institutional knowledge, toolsets, and contractor familiarity with VA’s capital investment process. Maintaining continuity is essential for efficient onboarding, stakeholder coordination, and meeting complex statutory and regulatory submission requirements.

The FY2028 / FY2029 Capital Budget Documents contract is not merely a technical support mechanism, it is a mission-critical strategic tool that underpins the execution of VA’s capital investment portfolio. Managed by Office of Construction and Facilities Management’s (CFM) Office of Real Property (ORP), this contract enables the development and submission of Non-IT Business Case Applications essential to executing congressionally approved Major Construction projects and Prospectus packages for Major Leases as required by U.S.C. § 8104 and Title 40 U.S.C. § 3301 et seq., while also ensuring alignment with OMB Circular A-11, Appendix B. These statutory frameworks and guidance govern how VA submits Major Construction projects and Major Leases for Congressional approval, and manages, and scores real property lease obligations, with direct implications for Veteran’s access to modern, safe, and effective medical facilities.

In accordance with the Bona-Fide Needs Rule (31 U.S.C. § 1502(a)), this contract addresses an immediate and legitimate need of the VA to support the development of a well-structured and justified Budget Requests for Major Construction Projects and Leases that will enhance facilities and services for Veterans. The services provided under this contract are essential to ensuring that VA funding requests align with VA’s strategic priorities, comply with federal budgeting and procurement laws, and optimize the allocation of taxpayer dollars. By conducting rigorous assessments and preparing detailed Non-IT Business Case Applications, this effort directly supports the VA’s mission to improve healthcare, benefits, and services for Veterans, as mandated under 38 U.S.C. § 7301 (Functions of the Veterans Health Administration) and the VA Major Construction and Lease Authorization Act.

Background: The SCIP process is the basis for VA’s current and out-year capital budget requests. The SCIP process includes development of 10-Year Action Plans and budget year Business Cases to close performance gaps (space, utilization, facility condition, etc.) to enhance healthcare and delivery of services and benefits for the nation’s Veterans.

In the late 1990s, VA began a dramatic change in the way it delivers services, shifting from an in-patient, hospital-based model to one that focuses on preventive care in outpatient settings. That shift has left VA with an increasing inventory of aging and obsolete facilities, many in locations where there is diminished demand. To build upon past capital planning efforts, and to address the problem of aging infrastructure in poor condition, lack of infrastructure in some locations and unused infrastructure in others, the Department has embarked on the SCIP process. SCIP is a significant and critical initiative that will enable VA to better adapt to changes in the environment, demographics, capabilities, medical technology, and health care delivery, thereby allowing VA to deliver the highest quality healthcare, benefits, and memorial services to our Nation’s veterans.

SCIP ensures that all resources will be scrutinized and considered at the corporate level, with equitable and consistent distribution across markets and competing capital needs to address gaps in our service delivery. SCIP provides the Secretary with a project list that is integrated across all administrations and programs (Major and Minor Construction, Leases, and Non- Recurring Maintenance) to ensure resources are allocated to address the most critical gaps.

With the strategic goal to improve the delivery of services and benefits to Veterans, the SCIP process will be the basis for the Department’s FY2028 Capital Budget Request. Unlike previous capital planning models, SCIP links planning efforts of the Administrations and Staff Offices for both capital and non-capital solutions and takes a long-term departmental approach. SCIP also encourages investments that ensure delivery of services in a Veteran-centric, forward-looking, and results-driven manner, while placing particular emphasis on improving access, maintaining our capital portfolio, increasing market penetration, reducing homelessness, and ameliorating issues confronting women Veterans.

Currently, VA has a significant funding backlog in construction projects and Facility Condition Assessment deficiencies, and many of its facilities are over-utilized, resulting in higher maintenance costs and inefficient resource usage.

Closing critical identified gaps will be the basis for FY2028 SCIP Business Case applications developed by the Administrations and Staff Offices. Business Cases will be prepared for Major Construction, Minor Construction, Major Leases, and Mid-Level Leases, since these are more complex and represent a higher risk to VA.

The Business Cases will be scored using the SCIP Decision Criteria Model resulting in a prioritized list of projects through VA’s governance process for inclusion in the FY2028 or FY2029 Budget Request. This scope of work is to assist VA with the preparation of Non-IT Business Case Applications for Major Construction projects and Prospectus and Budget Documents for Major and Mid-Level Leases for inclusion in VA’s FY2028 and FY2029 President’s Budget Requests.

BACKGROUND

The Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) Chief Information Officer (CIO) organization – through its Office of Information and Technology (OIT) – is responsible for integrating, securing, and modernizing the information technology that underpins VA’s delivery of care, benefits, and services to millions of Veterans. VA OIT currently staffs roughly 8,000 IT professionals, with budget authority of approximately $7.3 billion for IT systems in FY 2026. This includes significant investments in enterprise modernization programs such as Electronic Health Record Modernization (EHRM), Financial Management Business Transformation (FMBT), and other major enterprise solutions, while also addressing cybersecurity, cloud infrastructure, and legacy system retirement. 

As VA pursues these complex, multi-year IT transformations against a backdrop of workforce reorganization, reductions in staffing levels, and evolving technology demands, there is a clear need for structured, data-driven workforce gap analysis to inform strategic planning, risk management, and investment decisions that will help ensure mission success and continuity of services for Veterans. Specifically, VA OIT should consider acting on the following critical activities to ensure VA OIT’s ability to meet the urgent needs of current service delivery and plan for the future: 

Identify the future needs of the OIT workforce 

Identify skill areas that are lacking in OIT

Develop solutions to support workforce improvement initiatives 

Identify needs for future hiring

Below sections outline the comprehensive, multi-phase strategy required to identify and address workforce gaps for VA OIT. 

APPLICABLE DOCUMENTS

VA Handbook 6500, “Risk Management Framework for VA Information Systems VA Information Security Program,” February 24, 2021 (see VA Notice 25-01, dated October 15, 2024, “Update to VA Handbook 6500 Risk Management Framework for VA Information Systems VA Information Security Program”, and VA Notice 25-06, dated 3/18/25, “Amending VA Directive 6500 to incorporate M-24-15”)

SCOPE OF WORK

The Contractor shall conduct a comprehensive workforce analysis of the VA OIT to assess current capabilities, identify future workforce needs, and determine gaps between supply and demand. This effort will include reviewing strategic plans, analyzing workforce data, and developing actionable recommendations to address skill and capacity gaps. The Contractor shall deliver a roadmap of human capital solutions, including reskilling, recruiting, and organizational alignment strategies, to ensure OIT can meet mission objectives and modernization priorities.

PERFORMANCE DETAILS

PERFORMANCE PERIOD

The PoP shall be for a 12 month base period. Subsequent Option Periods will be determined prior to solicitation release.

There are 11 Federal holidays set by law (USC Title 5 Section 6103) that VA follows:

Under current definitions, five are set by date:

New Year's Day			January 1

Juneteenth				June 19

Independence Day			July 4

Veterans Day			November 11

Christmas Day			December 25

If any of the above falls on a Saturday, then Friday shall be observed as a holiday. Similarly, if one falls on a Sunday, then Monday shall be observed as a holiday.

The other six are set by a day of the week and month:

Martin Luther King's Birthday	Third Monday in January

Washington's Birthday	Third Monday in February

Memorial Day	Last Monday in May

Labor Day	First Monday in September

Columbus Day	Second Monday in October

Thanksgiving	Fourth Thursday in November 

PLACE OF PERFORMANCE

Tasks under this PWS shall be performed at Contractor facilities. The Contractor shall identify the Contractor’s place of performance in their proposal submission.

TRAVEL

There is no anticipated travel for this effort.

SPECIFIC TASKS AND DELIVERABLES

The Contractor shall perform the tasks described in Sections 5.1 through 5.6 to achieve the objectives outlined in this Performance Work Statement. Each task includes a description of required activities and identifies associated deliverables that support performance outcomes and enable Government oversight. The Contractor shall ensure all deliverables are complete, accurate, and provided in accordance with the format and schedule specified in the Notes to the Contracting Officer.

PROJECT MANAGEMENT

The Contractor shall provide integrated project management and task governance to ensure timely, coherent, and transparent execution of all activities under this PWS. The Contractor shall conduct the post-award kickoff meeting and furnish Kickoff Meeting Materials that establish the approach, roles, reporting cadence, and collaboration tools to be used across the engagement; these materials will serve as the foundational reference for stakeholders throughout performance. The Contractor shall develop and maintain a Project Management Plan (PMP) that articulates scope, governance, milestones, risks, communications, and dependencies and aligns with OIT leadership expectations; the PMP shall be kept current as the authoritative baseline for managing outcomes. The Contractor shall create and maintain an Integrated Master Schedule (IMS) that sequences tasks across Sections 5.2 through5.6 to drive deliverable readiness, highlight critical path items, and support oversight reporting to senior executives. To promote transparency and issue resolution, the Contractor shall provide Weekly Status Reports that summarize progress, risks/issues with mitigations, upcoming work, and Government Furnished equipment (GFE)/logistics changes, and shall prepare Executive Briefings upon Government request to synthesize decisions, options, and impacts for leadership forums.

Deliverables: 

Kickoff Meeting Materials

Project Management Plan

Integrated Master Schedule

Weekly Status Reports

Executive Briefings

FUTURE WORKFORCE DEMAND ANALYSIS

The Contractor shall analyze future OIT workforce demand to meet VA mission needs, enterprise modernization, cybersecurity, cloud adoption, and legacy system retirement—explicitly considering major initiatives such as EHRM and FMBT and other enterprise solutions driving technical skills requirements. The Contractor shall review OIT strategic plans and mission documentation, identify internal/external demand drivers (e.g., program roadmaps, technology trends, regulatory mandates), and translate enterprise technical demand into future workforce roles, skills, proficiencies, and capacity by product line and function. The Contractor shall develop a quantitative Workforce Demand Profile that estimates the volume and mix of roles/skills needed under plausible planning horizons; this profile will be positioned for executive use in resourcing and budget deliberations. The Contractor shall produce a Future-State Role and Skill Taxonomy that defines role families, core competencies, proficiency tiers, and example position profiles—standardizing terminology for downstream supply and gap analysis. To support decision flexibility, the Contractor shall produce multiple Workforce Demand Scenarios (e.g., baseline, accelerated modernization, constrained funding) with clear assumptions and sensitivity factors that enable leadership trade-offs.

Deliverables: 

Workforce Demand Profile

Future State Role and Skill Taxonomy

Workforce Demand Scenarios

CURRENT WORKFORCE SUPPLY AND CAPABILITY ASSESSMENT 

The Contractor shall assess OIT’s current workforce supply to determine skills, proficiencies, capacity, and risk factors that influence mission delivery across products and services. The Contractor shall collect and analyze available workforce data (e.g., HRSmart, training records, certifications), identify data gaps/limitations, and design a fit-for-purpose skills assessment using validated methodologies (e.g., role-based self-assessments corroborated by supervisor review and/or work samples) to establish current competency confidence levels. The resulting Workforce Supply Profile will quantify current capacity by role family, geography/organization, labor category, and proficiency tier, providing a baseline to compare against demand. The Contractor shall produce a Skills Inventory with Confidence Ratings that maps observed/validated skills to the taxonomy in Section 5.2, enabling rigorous analysis and reduce subjectivity in planning. In addition, the Contractor shall develop a Workforce Risk and Attrition Analysis that identifies near-term retirement exposure, critical-skill single-points-of-failure, institutional knowledge risks, and other factors (e.g., vacancy duration, recruitment pipeline constraints) that could degrade delivery. The Contractor shall review and validate key findings with OIT leadership to ensure enterprise alignment prior to finalization.

Deliverables: 

Workforce Supply Profile

Skills Inventory with Confidence Ratings

Workforce Risk and Attrition Analysis

WORKFORCE GAP AND SCENARIO ANALYSIS

The Contractor shall quantify gaps between the future workforce demand (Section 5.2) and current workforce supply (Section 5.3) across multiple scenarios to highlight where role mix, skill depth, or capacity shortfalls impede mission outcomes. The analysis shall compute gaps by role family and proficiency tier, overlay scenario assumptions (e.g., accelerated cloud migration or modernization delays), and translate differences into actionable implications for service delivery, modernization milestones, and product line readiness. The Contractor shall produce a comprehensive Workforce Gap Analysis Report that prioritizes gaps by impact and urgency, incorporates sensitivity analyses, and summarizes implications for planning windows (near-term, mid-term). The Contractor shall provide a Scenario Impact Assessment that shows how different modernization or budget trajectories alter the size, timing, and distribution of gaps to support leadership trade-off decisions. The Contractor shall develop a Mission Risk Assessment that connects unresolved gaps to operational risks (e.g., cybersecurity posture, schedule slip for enterprise programs, continuity of services), offering narrative and visualizations suitable for executive decision-making. Leadership feedback will be incorporated to finalize the analysis for governance use.

Deliverables: 

Workforce Gap Analysis Report

Scenario Impact Assessment

Mission Risk Assessment

WORKFORCE SOLUTIONS AND HUMAN CAPITAL PROGRAM DEVELOPMENT 

The Contractor shall design practical, prioritized solutions to close identified workforce gaps and strengthen OIT’s human capital programs within operational and fiscal constraints. The Contractor shall align proposed interventions to specific gap categories (skill depth, role rebalancing, capacity) and produce Workforce Solution Recommendations that specify the “what” (solution intent), “where” (target organizations/product lines), and “how” (sequenced actions and enabling governance). 

The Contractor shall develop a Human Capital Program Roadmap that integrates reskilling/upskilling pathways, competency-based recruiting/hiring strategies, retention initiatives, leadership/succession planning, and make-versus-buy strategies (Federal workforce, contractor support, shared services) into time-phased releases. 1. Description of Services.  
The contractor shall provide the 90th Missile Wing Leadership with products to help understand and make 
informed decisions on ways to improve the current Land Mobile Radio Network and identify any deficiencies 
within the system at FE Warren Air Force Base, Wyoming, in accordance with all applicable federal, state, 
local laws and regulations and this performance work statement (PWS). The contractor shall adhere to the 
established FE Warren speed limits to provide the best real world usage signal levels. 
 
1.1. Basic Services. Assess Very High Frequency (VHF) and Ultra High Frequency (UHF) Spectrum 
propagation and identify all areas where the uplink signal strength to the repeater is below -95 dBm (or 
other specified threshold) for both 5-watt and 50-watt transmitters. These areas will be defined as 'dead 
spots' for the purpose of this survey for the Wide Area Coverage Network at FE Warren AFB, throughout 
the entire missile complex, including all traveled roads to 15 Missile Alert Facilities & 150 Launch Facilities 
covering over 9600 Square miles. 
 
1.2. Specific Services. Provide statistical data on overall network capabilities and 
effective radiated Power Output (ERP) and Voltage Standing Wave Ratio (VSWR) of the 8 specified repeater 
sites. Reference Signals Received Power (RSRP) signal strength and Signal to Interference Ratio (SINR) for 
signal quality, for the entire system, not only the repeater sites.  
 
1.2.1. The contractor shall provide analysis of the existing bandwidth utilization and capacity of the 
microwave or fiber backhaul circuits connecting the 8 repeater sites and the master site. 
 
 
1.2.2. The contractor shall provide periodic status updates at the request of the Government and on a 
weekly basis. Updates shall be delivered to the RF Trans Shop. Communication details will be 
provided during post-award conference.
 
 
1.2.3. The contractor shall provide personnel with Motorola service certification prior to the start of on-
site performance. 
 
1.2.4. All data collected and all final deliverables under this PWS are considered Classified at 
the SECRET level. All contractor personnel who access the missile complex and handle survey data 
must possess a final, adjudicated SECRET security clearance at the time of contract award. 
 
 
1.2.5. The contractor shall provide electronic signal propagation maps addressing 5-watt & 50-watt radio 
uplink capabilities of the overall system, to include electronic signal coverage propagation maps 5-
watt & 50-watt radio uplink capabilities at each of the repeater sites showing overall coverage in 
all directions from strongest to weakest signals with the MAF and LF location overlaid onto the 
map.
 
 
1.2.6. The contractor shall provide a comprehensive report on deficiencies and performance 
recommendations. The report must include: a) An executive summary of findings. b) Analysis of 
each of the 8 repeater sites. c) A consolidated system-wide analysis. d) Prioritized 
recommendations for remediation of identified 'dead spots' or system deficiencies.
 
 
1.2.7. The contractor shall provide deliverables using the following file formats: GIS Data Layers in ESRI 
Shapefile (.shp) and Google Earth (.kml) format. Final reports and static maps shall be in Adobe 
Acrobat (.pdf) format. 
 

Page 4 of 14 
 
1.3. Handling and Safeguarding of SECRET and Classified Information. All data, analysis, 
reports, and electronic files generated as a result of this PWS are classified at the SECRET level. The 
contractor, including all employees and subcontractors, shall handle, safeguard, and transmit all 
classified information in strict accordance with this section and all applicable U.S. Government 
security regulations. 
 
1.3.1. Governing Directives. The contractor shall comply with all requirements for handling SECRET 
information as stipulated in the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM), 
DoD Manual 5200.01 ("DoD Information Security Program"), and Executive Order 13526. All 
personnel handling classified information must possess a final, adjudicated SECRET security 
clearance prior to accessing any classified materials related to this contract. 
 
1.3.2. Access and Need-to-Know. Access to SECRET information is strictly limited to contractor personnel 
who possess the appropriate security clearance and have a valid "need-to-know," as determined 
by the Government, to perform their contractual duties. The principle of "lawful government 
purpose" applicable to CUI does not apply; access is granted on a much more restrictive basis. 
 
1.3.3. Marking Requirements. All SECRET documents, data, and media (both physical and electronic) shall 
be conspicuously marked in accordance with DoD Manual 5200.01. This includes, but is not limited 
to: 
 
1.3.3.1. Overall classification markings at the top and bottom of each page. 
 
1.3.3.2. Portion markings for each paragraph to indicate its specific classification level. 
 
1.3.3.3. Markings on removable media, such as CDs, DVDs, and external drives. 
 
1.3.3.4. Appropriate cover sheets (e.g., SF 704, SECRET) shall be affixed to all classified documents 
when not stored in an approved container. 
 
1.3.4. Storage. After working hours, or when not under the direct control of an authorized individual, all 
SECRET material shall be stored in a General Services Administration (GSA)-approved security 
container (safe). Storing SECRET information in standard locked desks, cabinets, or unsecured 
rooms is strictly prohibited. 
 
1.3.5. Transmission. The transmission of SECRET information shall only occur through authorized and 
secure government channels. 
 
1.3.5.1. Electronic Transmission: SECRET information may only be transmitted electronically using 
a government-approved secure communications network, such as the Secret Internet Protocol 
Router Network (SIPRNet). Transmission over unclassified networks (including NIPRNet or the 
public internet), even with encryption such as TLS/HTTPS, is prohibited. 
 
1.3.5.2. Physical Transmission: Physical transfer of SECRET materials shall be conducted via a 
cleared courier on a GSA-approved courier card or by other means approved by the government's 
security office and compliant with NISPOM guidelines. Use of the U.S. Postal Service or other 
commercial carriers is prohibited. 
 

Page 5 of 14 
 
1.3.6. Disposition. The destruction of SECRET material, including all drafts, working papers, and 
electronic media, must be accomplished using government-approved methods that render the 
material completely unrecoverable and indecipherable. This includes using approved cross-cut 
shredders, burn bags, or other authorized destruction facilities. The methods used for destroying 
CUI or other unclassified information are not sufficient for SECRET material. 
 
1.3.7. Security Incidents and Unauthorized Disclosure. The contractor shall immediately report any 
suspected or actual compromise, loss, or unauthorized disclosure of SECRET information to the 
Contracting Officer (CO) and the sponsoring government security office. This includes any security 
violations or infractions, regardless of whether they resulted in a compromise. The contractor shall 
cooperate fully with any subsequent government investigation. 
 
1.4. Post-Award Conference.  The Contractor shall attend a Post-Award Conference with the 
Contracting Officer, Customer, and other Government entities, no later than ten (10) business days 
after the date of award.  The purpose of the Post Award Conference, which will be chaired by the 
Contracting Officer or Government PM, is to discuss the technical and contracting objectives of this 
contract and review the Contractor’s draft project plan.
 
 
1.4.1. Contractor’s Project Plan. The Contractor shall provide a draft Project Plan at the Post-Award 
Conference for Government review and comment.  The Project Plan shall include any designs, as 
required within this PWS.  The Contractor shall provide a final Project Plan to the Customer and 
Contracting Officer no later than five (5) business days after the Post-Award Conference.
 
 
1.5. Period of Performance (PoP). The contractor shall complete the Enterprise Land Mobile Radio 
Propagation Coverage Survey, including all testing, analysis, and submission of final deliverables, 
within 120 calendar days after the contract award date.

outlined in this PWS, the Contractor shall notify the Government they can no longer perform work. 90 
CS will validate that the weather no longer allows work to be performed within the specifications.  If

provided to support the winter suspension.  The project will be placed into suspension, and the 
remaining number of PoP days will be documented. When the weather starts to become workable 
weather, 90 CONS will start conversations with the contractor regarding when they can come back to 
work.  When the suspension is lifted, a new completion date will be established based on the 
remaining PoP days.

Statement of Work 
Operation Engage Reach and Impact Report 
 
 
Background 
In Fiscal Year 2020, the Drug Enforcement Administration deployed Operation Engage 
(https://www.dea.gov/operation-engage), which is a comprehensive approach that targets the top 
drug threat identified by DEA’s field divisions while continuing to focus on drug trafficking, 
violence, and crime reduction. Operation Engage’s goals are to identify and affect local drug 
threat enforcement priorities and drug use trends, support and contribute to local drug use 
prevention efforts, and bridge public safety and public health efforts. 
 
Each field division designates a city or region and tailors their drug use and misuse prevention 
efforts by identifying the drugs that affect individuals and families in the designated areas and 
identifying evidence-informed strategies that best fit the community’s needs. In Fiscal Year 
2025, Operation Engage was deployed in the following DEA field divisions: 
 
• Detroit Field Division: Toledo, Ohio 
• El Paso Field Division: Albuquerque, New Mexico 
• Los Angeles Field Division: Southern California 
• Miami Field Division: Ft. Lauderdale, Florida 
• New England Field Division: Lowell, Massachusetts 
• New Orleans Field Division: New Orleans, Louisiana 
• Philadelphia Field Division: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 
• Phoenix Field Division: Glendale, Arizona 
• St. Louis Field Division: St. Louis, Missouri 
• Seattle Field Division: Seattle, Washington 
• Washington, DC Field Division: Washington, DC, and select Maryland counties 
 
In each subsequent Option Period, DEA intends to deploy Operation Engage in all 23 of its field 
divisions, contingent upon the availability of funds and Administration priorities. 
 
Scope of Work 
To measure Operation Engage’s effectiveness, DEA established the following metrics: 
• Increase in number of public-private partnerships in each Operation Engage community to 
collaborate on efforts to reduce drug misuse-related problems. 
• Increase in community members' awareness of the scope of drug misuse-related problems in 
that community. 
• Increase in engagement by educators and parents in using science-based prevention 
materials, such as DEA's Operation Prevention, to prevent drug misuse in each Operation 
Engage community. 
• Community stakeholders' development of a formal strategic action plan to decrease drug 
misuse-related overdoses in each Operation Engage community. 
 
DEA also identified deliverables to be produced in each field division where Operation Engage 
is implemented. See Appendix A for a list of these deliverables and examples of associated 

2 
 
activities and Appendix B for the schedule of deliverables for this project. Note: One of the 
deliverables has a required activity for all Operation Engage locations. 
 
To document the reach and impact of Operation Engage, the vendor selected for this project shall 
analyze and report on these metrics and deliverables, through the following annual contract 
deliverables: 
 
• Deliverable 1: Kickoff Meeting and Workplan Development 
The vendor shall participate in a Kickoff Meeting with the Contracting Officer’s 
Representative and other DEA staff to review this project’s goals and the contractor’s 
workplan. The vendor shall develop the agenda, in consultation with the COR, and produce a 
draft and final summary of the Kickoff Meeting’s proceedings. 
• Deliverable 2: Metrics Analysis 
The vendor shall analyze all of the activities completed for each deliverable to determine the 
reach and impact in each Operation Engage location. 
• Deliverable 3: Key Stakeholder Interviews 
The vendor shall conduct up to five stakeholder interviews, in consultation with the COR, 
with a variety of individuals who were exposed to Operation Engage in each location, to 
obtain qualitative information on Operation Engage’s reach and impact in that location. 
• Deliverable 4: Reach and Impact Report 
The vendor will complete prior year 4 outstanding deliverable (2024 Reach and Impact Report) and 
additionally complete and submit year 5 (2025) Reach and Impact Report during the current period of 
performance (base option year). Based on analysis of each deliverable completed activities, and 
the information gained from the key stakeholder interviews, the vendor shall produce a draft 
and final report that highlights Operation Engage’s reach and impact and lessons learned. 
The reach and impact report also shall document each Operation Engage location’s progress 
toward meeting the four identified metrics as a result of their completed activities for each 
deliverable. The report shall combine clear and concise narrative with visually appealing 
graphics, and be appropriate for a wide variety of audiences, including prevention and 
treatment organizations; law enforcement organizations; local, state, national, and federal 
government officials; non-government community service organizations; educators; parents; 
and youth groups.  
• Deliverable 5: Lessons Learned Report 
The vendor shall produce a document that summarizes its lessons learned in conducting this 
project for DEA’s future reference in measuring Operation Engage’s reach and impact in 
other locations. 
 
Instructions to Offerors 
• Your bid shall consist of a Technical Proposal (must not exceed 20 double-spaced pages) on 
your plan to produce the deliverables identified in this SOW, and a Budget Proposal 
outlining all associated costs to produce the deliverables identified in this SOW. Your Budget 
Proposal shall include a quote for the Base Period and each Option Period. 
• The government estimates the contractor will need the following personnel to complete this 
project: Project Director (5 percent time), Senior Writer/Editor (15 percent time), Research 
Associate (20 percent time), and Graphic Designer (5 percent time). 

3 
 
• All information in the publication shall include citations to source materials. The contractor 
shall plan to gather relevant information from a variety of federal and non-federal sources. 
• The publication’s narrative shall be written in plain language. The contractor shall follow the 
Style Guide developed by DEA’s Community Outreach and Prevention Support Section, to 
be furnished upon contract award. 
• The publication shall not exceed 50 pages, inclusive of all graphics and appendices. 
• The contractor shall acquire all images, including copyright permissions, to include images in 
the print and online versions of the publication. The contractor may use appropriate stock 
photography or artwork provided appropriate releases are obtained. 
• The contractor will have significant experience in writing publications that focus on the reach 
and impact of community outreach activities to prevent drug use and misuse. 
• The publication will be made available in print and online versions. Therefore, the contractor 
shall ensure the online version is 508 compliant to post on www.dea.gov. 
• DEA’s logo shall be used on the publication. DEA shall provide logo upon contract award. 
• The contractor shall include a detailed description of its quality assurance plan to be used in 
developing the publication, to ensure it meets the highest standards relative to format, 
consistency, completeness, quality, and presentation. 
• The report shall be produced in Adobe InDesign (which is the software DEA uses) or another 
file format that is compatible with Adobe InDesign.

Base Period: August 29, 2026 – August 28, 2027 
Option Period 1: August 29, 2027 – August 28, 2028 
Option Period 2: August 29, 2028 – August 28, 2029

US Forest Service Forest Products Lab at 1 Gifford Pinchot Drive, Madison, WI and Request 
for Contractor Expressions of Interest (Ref. NAICS code 541330) 
1 NOTICE AND INVITATION 
US Forest Service is interested in pursuing a potential ESPC project on its Forest Products Laboratory 
campus at the following 4 locations: Main Building (building #1), Wood Fiber Products Lab (building 
#33), Wood Chemistry Lab (building #34), and Centennial Research Facility (building #50) at its 1 Gifford 
Pinchot Drive Madison, WI 53726 location.    
This notice of opportunity invites current holders of the Department of Energy’s (DOE’s) Fourth 
Generation ESPC indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity (IDIQ) contract to submit a written response (an 
expression of interest) to be considered for contractor selection for this potential task order award. This 
notice is limited to contract holders who are interested in being prime contractors on this project. 
Responses from vendors interested in being subcontractors will not be accepted. 
The scope of any task order (TO) awarded for this project is the buildings and facilities as identified in 
this notice.  While certain energy and water conservation measures (ECMs) will be included at the time 
of the original TO award, United States Forest Service may, at any time during the performance period, 
request the selected ESCO to do further analysis to determine whether expansion of ECMs included in 
the original TO or additional ECMs for the identified buildings and facilities are feasible. If deemed viable 
and desirable, United States Forest Service may incorporate the additional ECMs into this project by way 
of TO modification. 
The Energy Service Company (ESCO) will be required to use eProjectBuilder (ePB) in developing the ESPC 
project and presenting baselines, estimated savings, and financial schedules to agency.   ePB is a free 
web-based system for entering and tracking ESPC data through the life of a project. It can be accessed 
at: https://eprojectbuilder.lbl.gov. 
2 FACILITY OVERVIEW 
2.1  Forest Products Laboratory Mission 
The mission of the Forest Products Lab (FPL) is to develop science and technology to conserve, extend, 
and sustainably utilize forest resources to improve the health, diversity, and productivity of the Nation’s 
forests to meet the needs of current and future generations.  
2.2 Facility Description 


The FPL campus is in Madison, WI. This effort is focused on four buildings that span 359,294 SF. Below is 
table (table #1) and site map (Figure 1) of the campus that depicts the four buildings that are included in 
project. This section also includes general descriptions for each of the buildings included in this project.

Building 1 (Main Building) 
An industrial modern, six-story U-shape building constructed in 1932 and annexes were added in 1935 
and in the 1950s. This is an historic building and serves as the primary research and administrative 
headquarters for wood utilization research and houses approximately 140 occupants. Combination of 
office and laboratory space, including an herbarium for forest mycology research. Building provides 
approximately 196,286 square feet of conditioned space.  


The building has brick walls with exterior precast concrete panels. The interior insulation is at an 
estimated R-value of R-5 within metal stud framing and finished with gypsum wallboard. The roof is a 
built-up roof with light colored stone and approximately R-11 insulation. The roof is approximately 16 
years old. Windows are a clear double-hung, single-pane storm window with metal frame. The windows 
are leaky and difficult to open and close as most locking mechanisms have malfunctioned. Roughly 20% 
are cracked. Replacing ground-floor windows are a priority.  
Most interior lights are recessed fixtures with T8 fluorescent, LEDs, compact fluorescent lamps, and 
some high bay metal halide fixtures. The interior lighting for offices is controlled by wall switches. 
There are small laboratories throughout the building. Each standard laboratory has laboratory 
equipment and fume hoods. Shop area contains large professional machinery. 
The ground floor and the 5th floor of the building are served by four variable air volume (VAV) systems 
with how water reheat. The offices on the 2nd, 3rd and 4th floor are served by 4-pipe fan coil units (FCUs). 
The FCUs’ fans have three-speeds that could be set by occupants. Fresh air for the spaces on 2nd to 4th 
floor is provided through windows. The FCUs are approximately 16 years old. 
The building has one steam-to-hot water heat exchanger with 45-gallon tank for domestic hot water. 
Heat exchangers are scheduled to be replaced in FY27. Building HVAC systems are controlled by mixed 
components of Allerton and Johnson Controls building automation system (BAS). There are known 
problems with incompatibility between the Allerton and Johnson Controls system. Zone temperature 
was controlled by thermostats in various locations throughout the building. The cooling and heating 
setpoints were 73°F and 70°F, respectively. There were potential problems with temperature sensors for 
spaces served by FCUs as the temperature setpoints could not be overridden, and the temperature 
setback could not be implemented. 
A number of stainless steel sinks are corroded and leaking. 
Building 33 (Fiber Products Laboratory) 
This is a rectangular building that is approximately 41,457 square feet in size. This building has a low 
slope built up roof that was installed in 2016 and a brick veneer with CMU backup that was installed in 
1967.  The existing HVAC system of FPL’s Building 33 and 34 uses variable volume supply and exhaust. 
Laboratory space includes specialized fiber and chemical sciences research. Building 33 has a 100 gallon 
expansion tank tied to its heating system that was installed in 1967.  
The 200-ton rotary screw liquid chilled water system was installed in 2000 and serves both Buildings 33 
and 34. There are three 5000 CFM air handling units that were installed in the 1980s. The Veteran 
Administration has facilities nearby and is potentially interested in a partnership to develop a shared 
chilled water solution. 
Building 34 (Wood Chemistry Laboratory) 
This is a rectangular building that is approximately 31,469 square feet in size. This building includes 
laboratory space supporting analytical chemistry and microbial and biochemical research. Building 34 
has a low slope built up roof that was installed in 2016.  This building has a hot water distribution system 
that was installed in 1988 and it shares cooling with Building 33. 
A number of sinks and showers are corroded and leaking. 
Building 50 (Centennial Research Facility) 
A 90,082 square-foot facility supporting advanced, collaborative research. This building was built in 2010 
and has office, conditioned storage, and laboratory space for testing wood-framed buildings, wood 
members, wood preservatives, and wood-based and wood-plastic products. Heat exchangers are 

scheduled to be replaced in FY27. Bldg 50’s roof warranty recently expired and needs to be replaced. 
This location is considered the best option for potential solar photovoltaics. 
All Buildings 
Madison Gas & Electric Company provides power at 12.47 KV and distributes via transformers. 
University of Wisconsin provides steam at 175 psig via a 6” main. Condensate is returned via a 3” 
condensate pipe. Steam enters at Bldg 5 (Steam Plant) and uses its distribution headers. Buildings 33 
and 34 are the only buildings with natural gas, however this is only used for laboratory purposes and is 
considered negligible. City of Madison provides water to the FPL main campus via an 8” water main. City 
of Madison provides sewer service via a 10” sewer line to all facility buildings. The current control 
system for all buildings is out-of-date and frequently inoperable; a user-friendly replacement/upgrade is 
strongly desired.

1.0 INTRODUCTION AND GENERAL INFORMATION: 
 
1.1 INTRODUCTION 
This Performance Work Statement (PWS) supports Naval Information Warfighting Development 
Center (NIWDC) warfighting capabilities with specific focus towards Electronic Warfare Data 
(EWD)production (using the Navy Information Operations Database (NIODB)) currently operated 
on an Amazon Web Service (AWS) Impact Level (IL6) cloud hosting environment.  NIODB is a 
Navy approved source of parametric, and order of battle data used in the development of Electronic 
Warfare (EW) System Libraries.  Aiding the warfighter with a single source of authoritative EW 
data, it improves threat and own force identification, enables Anti-Ship Missile Defense, enhances 
interoperability, and improves mission planning through improved threat data fidelity.  OPNAV 
Instruction 3430.23D provides policy for United States Fleet Forces Command ( USFFC) and 
Naval Information Forces ( NAVIFOR) execution of the Electronic Warfare Reprogrammable 
Systems Support Program.  NIWDC EWD is NAVIFOR designated EW Functional Data Manager 
and is the primary organization for this support.

Identification of Roadway Design and Infrastructure Factors Influencing ADAS 
Systems in Mitigating Rural Roadway Departure Crashes 
 
1.0 Overview 
 
This is a non-personal services purchase order to provide services for identifying roadway design 
and infrastructure factors influencing Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) in mitigating 
rural roadway departure crashes. The Government will not exercise any supervision or control over 
the service providers performing the services herein. The Contractor is responsible to the 
Government as defined in this Performance Work Schedule (PWS) and must perform to the 
standards herein. 
 
1.1 Background 
 
The mission of the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) is to improve safety and mobility on 
our nation’s highways through national leadership, innovation, and program delivery. As part of this 
mission, FHWA allocates funding to develop and deliver technical assistance, research, data 
analysis, and training aimed for reducing roadway departure (RwD) crashes and fatalities through 
the implementation of safety action plans and proven safety countermeasures. With the rapid growth 
of vehicles with ADAS, it is critical to investigate the infrastructures required to support these 
systems and to assess their safety effectiveness in reducing RwD crashes. 
 
As human error accounts for more than 90% of traffic crashes, Advanced Driver Assistance Systems 
(ADAS) are expected to provide significant safety benefits by supporting drivers with timely 
warnings and/or active interventions, thereby reducing traffic crashes, and migrating the risk of fatal 
and serious injuries. In recent years, continuous technological advancements, and growing consumer 
awareness of safety have accelerated adoption of new vehicles equipped with Lane Departure 
Warning (LDW), Lane Keeping Assistance (LKA), and Lane Centering Assistance (LCA) features 
as standard. These systems, designed to address RwD crashes, are expected to play a significant role 
in reducing fatalities and serious injuries associated with such crashes.  
 
However, these expected safety benefits are based on the assumption that roadway geometry and 
infrastructure factors fully support these technologies, which is not always available. Existing 
roadway infrastructure, particularly rural roadways, remains insufficient to fully support the 
functionality and safety potential of evolving ADAS technologies. Many rural roadways lack 
consistent and well-maintained lane marking, adequate lighting, and uniform signage, which are 
essential for sensor-based systems to function reliably. In addition, geometric variations such as 
sharp curves, narrow lane and shoulder widths, and unpaved edges introduce challenges for vehicle 
detection and control algorithms. 
 
This purchase order aims to investigate and identify roadways characteristics, geometric design, and 
infrastructure factors necessary to optimize the safety benefits of relevant RwD prevention ADAS 
technologies for reducing RwD crashes in rural roads. It also quantifies the potential safety benefits 

 
 
6 
 
of these systems and identifies corresponding and prioritized infrastructure improvements to 
maximize those benefits.  
 
1.2 Objective 
 
The objective of this purchase order is to conduct a comprehensive review and assessment of geometric 
design elements and infrastructure factors that contribute to optimize the performance of RwD prevention 
ADAS technologies such as LDW, LKA, and LCA. By systematically reviewing and analyzing these 
contribution factors, this study seeks to provide evidence-based insights and actionable recommendation to 
improve roadway geometric design and infrastructure in support of vehicles equipped with these ADAS 
features, thereby maximizing their safety benefits in reducing RwD crashes and fatalities, particularly on rural 
roadways.  
 
This purchase order seeks to support FHWA mission to improve safety on our nation’s roadways in 
accordance with 23 U.S.C. §503(b)(1)(A, B, C & D); 23 U.S.C. §503(b)(2)(B)(i, ii, iii, iv, v & vi); 
23 U.S.C. §503(b)(2)(C)(i, ii, iii, vi, & viii); and 23 U.S.C. §503(b)(3)(B)(ii). 
 
1.3 Detailed Requirement  
 
The Contractor shall provide all personnel, equipment, supplies, facilities, transportation, tools, 
materials, supervision, and other items and non-personal services necessary to perform this purchase 
order. Also, project management, administrative support and periodic or recurring progress meetings 
shall be considered integral to each task as described here in. To accomplish the objectives of this 
order, the Contractor shall complete the following tasks: 
 
TASK 1: Attend Kick-Off Meeting 
 
The Contractor shall coordinate and facilitate a kick-off meeting with the Technical Point of Contact 
(TPOC) and others as appropriate within two weeks of award date. The Kick-Off meeting will be 
held virtually and will discuss the overall project to ensure that desired outcomes are understood and 
achieved. The Contractor shall prepare a draft work plan that is consistent with the technical quote, 
and provide a detailed schedule of milestones and deliverables. The Contractor shall send the draft 
agenda, presentation, and work plan to the TPOC one-week in advance of the kick-off meeting, at 
the latest, for review. After the kick-off meeting, the Contractor shall - submit a revised final work 
plan and work breakdown structure that incorporates comments and feedback provided from FHWA. 
In addition, the Contractor shall arrange bi-weekly check-in meetings with TPOC and FHWA’s 
stakeholders to discuss the progress, possible risks, and comments under this order. 
 
Deliverables: 
- Kick-Off Meeting Agenda, Draft work Plan and Draft Kick-off Meeting presentation 
- Kick-Off Meeting 
- Kick-Off Meeting Summary Note 
- Revised Work Plan 
- Bi-weekly Check-in Meeting  
- Bi-weekly Check-in Meeting Summary Note 
- Quarterly Progress Report 
 

 
 
7 
 
TASK 2: Collect, Extract, Integrate, and Evaluate Roadway Geometric Design Elements and 
Infrastructure Factors Affecting RwD Avoidance ADAS 
 
The Contractor shall conduct a comprehensive data-driven process to collect, extract, integrate, and 
analyze various data from various resources including, but are not limited to, geometric design 
elements, infrastructure features, historical crash data and vehicle trajectory data to identify and 
evaluate factors affecting the safety performance of RwD avoidance ADAS features on rural roads. 
 
The Contractor shall identify, extract and compile roadway geometric design elements and 
infrastructure features that are potentially associated with operational effectiveness of RwD 
prevention ADAS features, which may include, but are not limited to, horizontal and vertical 
alignment characteristics, advanced signs and delineation, pavement and longitudinal markings (e.g., 
color, function, widths and patterns), roadside features, lane configuration, shoulder and median 
features, etc. through the integrated use of Geographic Information System (GIS) and image-based 
feature extraction processes. The Contractor shall use roadway map resource incorporating the 
Highway Performance Monitoring Systems (HPMS), or All Road Network of Linear Reference Data 
(ARNOLD), or comparable GIS-based Linear Reference System (LRS) developed and maintained 
by Federal and State agencies to ensure consistent spatial alignment and accurate location 
referencing across roadway networks.  
 
The Contractor’s proposed and performed image-based feature extraction process shall employ 
vision technologies (e.g., aerial or street-level imagery) to detect, classify, assess, and extract 
roadway geometric design and infrastructure attributes. Furthermore, the extracted roadway and 
infrastructure attributes must be integrated with the GIS LRS framework, enabling a repeatable and 
scalable workflow that accurately assigns spatial attributes along roadways.
